true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second definition of `OptimizedImage.downsize` overwrites the 4/5-argument version

Ruby does not support method overloading by arity. Defining `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` on line 149 completely replaces `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` defined on line 145. Any caller invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height)` with 4 arguments will now bind `dimensions` to `max_width` and `opts` to `max_height` (causing `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` / `opts[:allow_animation]` to raise `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer`), and any 5-argument call with `opts` will raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (5 for 3..4)`.

`UploadsController#create_upload` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. For a `.gif` file with `allow_animation` enabled, `downsize_instructions_animated` delegates to `resize_instructions_animated`, which invokes `gifsicle` with `--resize-fit 80%`. `gifsicle`'s `--resize-fit` option only accepts `WxH` pixel dimensions (scaling by a factor in `gifsicle` requires `--scale`), so `gifsicle` exits with a non-zero status and animated GIFs are never downsized.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`tempfile.size` and `tempfile` FD become stale when `OptimizedImage.downsize` replaces the file on disk

`Tempfile#size` calls `@tmpfile.stat.size` (`fstat` on the open file descriptor), not `File.size(tempfile.path)`. Inside `OptimizedImage.downsize`, `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` writes to a temporary file and atomically renames it over `tempfile.path`. Once that rename happens, `tempfile`'s open file descriptor still points to the old, unlinked inode while subsequent `convert` runs modify the new inode at `tempfile.path`. As a result, `tempfile.size` in the `while` condition and in `Upload.create_for(..., tempfile, filename, tempfile.size, ...)` reports the stale size from the old inode, and reading from the `tempfile` IO object reads the pre-replacement contents. In addition, the loop does not check the boolean return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`, so unsupported images (such as SVGs, which pass `FileHelper.is_image?`) or failed conversions will pointlessly retry all 5 attempts.

`ActiveModel::Serializer` requires conditional inclusion methods to end with a question mark (`include_website_name?`). Because the method is defined as `def include_website_name`, it is never called by the serializer, causing `:website_name` to always be serialized in the JSON output (even as `nil` when the user has no website).

Adding `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` (and removing the manual `include_website_name` method) will automatically define `include_website_name?` with both the `restrict_user_fields?` check and the `.present?` check.

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` and `ensure_loaded!` do not normalize `locale` to a symbol

In `FallbackLocaleList#[]`, `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` leaves `locale` as-is while converting `SiteSetting.default_locale` and `:en` to symbols. When `I18n.t(key, locale: "en")` or `I18n.fallbacks["fr"]` is called with a string locale (such as `SiteSetting.default_locale` or `user.effective_locale`), `.uniq` does not deduplicate `"en"` and `:en` (returning `["en", :en]`), causing duplicate lookups on missing keys. Likewise, `I18n.ensure_loaded!` and `I18n.load_locale` in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb` do not convert `locale` with `.to_sym`, so passing a string locale when the symbol locale is already in `@loaded_locales` will reload all YAML files for that locale a second time.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are not loaded when `I18n.t` is called outside `ApplicationController` or with a `:locale` option

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only called in `ApplicationController#set_locale`, while `I18n.translate` in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb` only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`. When `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks#translate` iterates over `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`, it calls `super(fallback, key, options)` directly on `I18n.backend`, bypassing `I18n.translate`. As a result, whenever `I18n.t` is called outside a controller action (e.g. in Sidekiq jobs, `UserNotifications` mailers, rake tasks, or specs), after `I18n.reload!`, or with an explicit `I18n.t(key, locale: ...)` / `I18n.with_locale(...)`, the fallback locales (or the passed `:locale`) are never loaded into `I18n.backend`. Fallback lookups then fail with missing translations, and for zero-argument `I18n.t(key)` calls, the missing-translation result gets cached in `@cache`. Ensuring fallback locales are loaded inside `load_locale`/`translate` in `translate_accelerator.rb` (including when `options[:locale]` is passed) avoids this.

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` in `sentry.utils.cache.cache` for 60 seconds keyed by `organization.id` and `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. This contradicts `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s documented behavior of reading the allowlist fresh each time, causes stale eligibility results when the option changes (including across tests that mock or update `options` for the same organization and project IDs), and adds an unnecessary external cache lookup on every stats query when `sentry.options.get` already caches option values in memory with automatic invalidation.

Substring check in `_is_error_focused_query` matches negated or compound queries

`_is_error_focused_query` checks `if "event.type:error" in query:` using a raw substring match on the query string. A query that explicitly excludes errors such as `!event.type:error` (for example, when querying transactions) or a disjunction such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` still contains the substring `"event.type:error"` and will erroneously trigger error upsampling on non-error events.

`upsampled_count` does not fall back to 1 when `sample_weight` is null or unset

`upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`, assuming every error event in an allowlisted project has a populated `sample_weight`. In practice, unsampled error events, events ingested before client error sampling was enabled for the project, or events from SDKs that do not send `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` have `sample_weight` as `NULL` or `0` (or `<= 1`). The aggregation should fall back to `1` when `sample_weight` is null or not greater than `1` (e.g., `if(greater(sample_weight, 1), sample_weight, 1)` or `greatest(ifNull(sample_weight, 1), 1)`).

1. On line 142, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` uses `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime` (making `end` identical to `start`), so slots that start at `workingHour.endTime` or extend past `workingHour.endTime` are not rejected.
2. If a host does not work at all on `slotStartTime.day()` (for example, a fixed host is off on Tuesday while a round-robin host works Tuesday), `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` is `false` for all entries, so `workingHours.find(...)` returns `undefined` and the host is treated as available all day.
3. If a host has more than one `workingHours` entry for the same day (either from multiple shifts like 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, or because `getWorkingHours` splits schedules that cross 00:00 UTC into `[0, endTime]` and `[startTime, 1439]`), `workingHours.find(...)` returns a match as soon as a slot is outside any single entry, rejecting all slots for that host on that day.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Date override validation in `checkIfIsAvailable` uses `===` on `Dayjs` objects, misses partial overlaps, and breaks with multiple overrides or UTC day boundaries

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` check in `checkIfIsAvailable` has several logic bugs:

1. Line 114 compares `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` using `===` between two distinct `Dayjs` object instances, which always evaluates to `false` instead of `.isSame(...)`. For an all-day unavailable override (where `start` and `end` are both 00:00), this check never triggers and a slot starting at 00:00 is not rejected.
2. Lines 117-125 only reject slots where `slotEndTime <= overrideStart` or `slotStartTime > overrideEnd`. Slots that start before `overrideStart` and end inside the override, slots that start inside the override and end after `overrideEnd`, and slots that start exactly at `overrideEnd` are not rejected.
3. Using `.find(...)` to reject a slot if it is outside any matching override on that day breaks when a user defines multiple override ranges on the same day (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00), because a slot inside the first range is outside the second range.
4. Comparing `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` compares UTC calendar dates rather than the date in `organizerTimeZone`. When the organizer's local day spans two UTC dates (e.g. `America/Los_Angeles`), slots on the override day that fall after 00:00 UTC have a different UTC date than `date.start` and fail to match the override, while slots from the previous local day that fall after 00:00 UTC falsely match the override.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override timezone shift wraps modulo 24h and matches the wrong day when overrides cross midnight in the invitee's timezone

In `getSlots`, shifting `override.start` and `override.end` by `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` and taking `.hour() * 60 + .minute()` wraps around at 24:00 (0 minutes):

1. If the timezone offset pushes `override.end` to or past midnight in the invitee's timezone while `override.start` remains before midnight (for example, a 14:00-18:00 UTC override viewed from `Asia/Tokyo` UTC+9 is 23:00-03:00, yielding `startTime = 1380` and `endTime = 180`, or an override ending at 24:00 invitee time yielding `endTime = 0`), `startTime >= endTime` and `buildSlots` discards the range (`if (start >= end) continue`), returning no slots.
2. `activeOverrides` (line 206) checks `dayjs.utc(override.start).isBetween(startOfInviteeDay, startOfInviteeDay.endOf("day"), null, "[)")` using the unshifted `override.start` (which encodes organizer local time as UTC). When the timezone difference shifts the override into the previous or next calendar date in the invitee's timezone, `activeOverrides` does not match on the invitee date where the slots actually fall, and when it does match, `buildSlots` anchors the wrapped `startTime` to `startOfInviteeDay`, shifting the resulting UTC slot timestamps by 24 hours.

Early return on `dateOverrideExist` bypasses busy-time checks and allows double bookings

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, when a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot falls within the override's hours, `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` returns immediately before reaching `return busy.every(...)` at line 153. Because `getTimeSlots` does not filter out busy times, `checkIfIsAvailable` is the only place where existing Cal.com bookings and external calendar busy blocks are checked. Returning `true` here causes all busy times to be ignored on any day that has a date override, allowing hosts to be double-booked. `dateOverrideExist` should only skip the `workingHours` check (`if (!dateOverrideExist) { ... }`) and still fall through to `busy.every(...)`.

false_positives.candidate:
Background commit_thread invokes Arroyo's non-thread-safe commit callback concurrently

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background `commit_thread` that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the Arroyo `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor`'s commit callback (`KafkaConsumer.stage_positions` and `KafkaConsumer.commit_offsets`) is not thread-safe and mutates internal offset dictionaries and consumer state without locks on the assumption that it is only called from the main `StreamProcessor` thread (e.g., inside `submit()` or `poll()`). Calling `commit` from a background thread races with `StreamProcessor._run_once()` polling and committing on the main thread. Performing the periodic commit check inside `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` (and once at shutdown after workers drain) keeps all consumer operations on the main thread.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued items and stops commit thread before workers drain

There are two issues in the shutdown sequence across `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (lines 335-339) and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (lines 231-244):
1. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. While `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is intended to let workers drain remaining queued items until `q.get()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown:` on each iteration (line 129). As a result, each worker exits immediately after finishing at most one in-flight item, dropping all other items still queued.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and does not perform a final commit afterward. Offsets completed since the last 1-second commit tick or during queue draining are never committed.

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets skips over uncommitted offset gaps after a commit

In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed()`, all offsets `<= offset` are removed from `self.all_offsets[partition]` (line 105). In `get_committable_offsets()`, the scan starts at `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` where `min_offset = min(all_offsets)` (lines 83-86). If offset 100 is committed and pruned from `all_offsets`, and offsets 102 and 103 are completed while offset 101 has not yet been added, `min_offset` is `102`, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`. The loop then starts at 102, completely skips the missing offset 101, and reports 103 as committable. Once `partition in self.last_committed`, the contiguous check must start at `last_committed + 1`, not `max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`.

Queues in FixedQueuePool are unbounded, providing no backpressure to StreamProcessor

Although `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring states that it provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", `FixedQueuePool` initializes each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded). In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka and calls `strategy.submit(message)` as fast as messages arrive until `submit` raises `MessageRejected`. Because `submit()` only decodes the payload in memory and pushes a `WorkItem` (including the full raw `Message`) onto an unbounded queue without ever raising `MessageRejected`, any slowdown in downstream worker processing will cause the consumer to buffer an unbounded number of messages and offsets in memory.

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance (line 133) and reuses it across `create_with_partitions` calls (line 255). In Arroyo, whenever a Kafka consumer group rebalance occurs, `StreamProcessor` revokes partitions by calling `strategy.close()` and `strategy.join()` on the current strategy, and then calls `factory.create_with_partitions(...)` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (line 338 of `queue_consumer.py`), all worker threads in `self.queue_pool` exit and all `queue.Queue` instances are permanently shut down. After the rebalance, the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` receives the already-shut-down `queue_pool`; every subsequent `submit()` call hits `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception` and marks the offset completed (lines 317-325 of `queue_consumer.py`), the consumer will silently drop all messages after any rebalance while still committing their offsets to Kafka.

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance (line 133) and reuses it across `create_with_partitions` calls (line 255). In Arroyo, whenever a Kafka consumer group rebalance occurs, `StreamProcessor` revokes partitions by calling `strategy.close()` and `strategy.join()` on the current strategy, and then calls `factory.create_with_partitions(...)` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (line 338 of `queue_consumer.py`), all worker threads in `self.queue_pool` exit and all `queue.Queue` instances are permanently shut down. After the rebalance, the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` receives the already-shut-down `queue_pool`; every subsequent `submit()` call hits `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception` and marks the offset completed (lines 317-325 of `queue_consumer.py`), the consumer will silently drop all messages after any rebalance while still committing their offsets to Kafka.

While `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is intended to let workers drain remaining queued items until `q.get()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown:` on each iteration (line 129). As a result, each worker exits immediately after finishing at most one in-flight item, dropping all other items still queued.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and does not perform a final commit afterward. Offsets completed since the last 1-second commit tick or during queue draining are never committed.

In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed()`, all offsets `<= offset` are removed from `self.all_offsets[partition]` (line 105). If offset 100 is committed and pruned from `all_offsets`, and offsets 102 and 103 are completed while offset 101 has not yet been added, `min_offset` is `102`, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`. The loop then starts at 102, completely skips the missing offset 101, and reports 103 as committable. Once `partition in self.last_committed`, the contiguous check must start at `last_committed + 1`, not `max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`.

Background commit_thread invokes Arroyo's non-thread-safe commit callback concurrently

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background `commit_thread` that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the Arroyo `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor`'s commit callback (`KafkaConsumer.stage_positions` and `KafkaConsumer.commit_offsets`) is not thread-safe and mutates internal offset dictionaries and consumer state without locks on the assumption that it is only called from the main `StreamProcessor` thread (e.g., inside `submit()` or `poll()`). Calling `commit` from a background thread races with `StreamProcessor._run_once()` polling and committing on the main thread. Performing the periodic commit check inside `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` (and once at shutdown after workers drain) keeps all consumer operations on the main thread.

Queues in FixedQueuePool are unbounded, providing no backpressure to StreamProcessor

Although `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring states that it provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", `FixedQueuePool` initializes each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded). In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka and calls `strategy.submit(message)` as fast as messages arrive until `submit` raises `MessageRejected`. Because `submit()` only decodes the payload in memory and pushes a `WorkItem` (including the full raw `Message`) onto an unbounded queue without ever raising `MessageRejected`, any slowdown in downstream worker processing will cause the consumer to buffer an unbounded number of messages and offsets in memory.

false_positives.candidate:
Shutting down shared FixedQueuePool on strategy close breaks consumer after partition rebalance

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance (line 133) and reuses it across `create_with_partitions` calls (line 255). In Arroyo, whenever a Kafka consumer group rebalance occurs, `StreamProcessor` revokes partitions by calling `strategy.close()` and `strategy.join()` on the current strategy, and then calls `factory.create_with_partitions(...)` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (line 338 of `queue_consumer.py`), all worker threads in `self.queue_pool` exit and all `queue.Queue` instances are permanently shut down. After the rebalance, the new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` receives the already-shut-down `queue_pool`; every subsequent `submit()` call hits `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception` and marks the offset completed (lines 317-325 of `queue_consumer.py`), the consumer will silently drop all messages after any rebalance while still committing their offsets to Kafka.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued items and stops commit thread before workers drain

There are two issues in the shutdown sequence across `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (lines 335-339) and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (lines 231-244):
1. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. While `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is intended to let workers drain remaining queued items until `q.get()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown:` on each iteration (line 129). As a result, each worker exits immediately after finishing at most one in-flight item, dropping all other items still queued.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` stops and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and does not perform a final commit afterward. Offsets completed since the last 1-second commit tick or during queue draining are never committed.

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets skips over uncommitted offset gaps after a commit

In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed()`, all offsets `<= offset` are removed from `self.all_offsets[partition]` (line 105). In `get_committable_offsets()`, the scan starts at `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` where `min_offset = min(all_offsets)` (lines 83-86). If offset 100 is committed and pruned from `all_offsets`, and offsets 102 and 103 are completed while offset 101 has not yet been added, `min_offset` is `102`, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`. The loop then starts at 102, completely skips the missing offset 101, and reports 103 as committable. Once `partition in self.last_committed`, the contiguous check must start at `last_committed + 1`, not `max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`.

Background commit_thread invokes Arroyo's non-thread-safe commit callback concurrently

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background `commit_thread` that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the Arroyo `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor`'s commit callback (`KafkaConsumer.stage_positions` and `KafkaConsumer.commit_offsets`) is not thread-safe and mutates internal offset dictionaries and consumer state without locks on the assumption that it is only called from the main `StreamProcessor` thread (e.g., inside `submit()` or `poll()`). Calling `commit` from a background thread races with `StreamProcessor._run_once()` polling and committing on the main thread. Performing the periodic commit check inside `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` (and once at shutdown after workers drain) keeps all consumer operations on the main thread.

Queues in FixedQueuePool are unbounded, providing no backpressure to StreamProcessor

Although `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring states that it provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", `FixedQueuePool` initializes each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded). In Arroyo, `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka and calls `strategy.submit(message)` as fast as messages arrive until `submit` raises `MessageRejected`. Because `submit()` only decodes the payload in memory and pushes a `WorkItem` (including the full raw `Message`) onto an unbounded queue without ever raising `MessageRejected`, any slowdown in downstream worker processing will cause the consumer to buffer an unbounded number of messages and offsets in memory.

Because `submit()` only decodes the payload in memory and pushes a `WorkItem` (including the full raw `Message`) onto an unbounded queue without ever raising `MessageRejected`, any slowdown in downstream worker processing will cause the consumer to buffer an unbounded number of messages and offsets in memory.
